questions.q: How is a wildlife corridor an example of a 'design solution' for protecting biodiversity?

It's a deliberately engineered/protected solution to reconnect fragmented habitats caused by human development
It only helps humans, not wildlife

Social Studies|6.1.1.title: What Makes a Civilization?
Social Studies|6.1.1.goal: You're comparing three early civilizations — Sumer, Egypt, and China — to find the ingredients every civilization needs: cities, government, writing, and more.
Social Studies|6.1.1.why: Once you can spot these ingredients, you'll recognize them in every society you study this year, from ancient empires to the modern world.

Social Studies|6.1.2.title: Where Did the World's Religions Begin?
Social Studies|6.1.2.goal: You'll get a quick tour of the origins of the major world religions and see how belief systems shaped early societies.
Social Studies|6.1.2.why: Religion has influenced art, law, and government for thousands of years — knowing where these traditions started helps explain a lot of world history.

Social Studies|6.1.3.title: Geography Shapes Civilizations
Social Studies|6.1.3.goal: You're using maps to see how rivers and land shaped where early civilizations grew — the Nile, the Tigris and Euphrates, and the Indus River valley.
Social Studies|6.1.3.why: Geography decided where people could farm, trade, and build cities — it's still one of the biggest reasons history unfolded where it did.

Social Studies|6.1.4.title: Ancient Economies and Technology
Social Studies|6.1.4.goal: You'll look at how early civilizations traded, farmed, and invented things like writing and currency to keep their societies running.
Social Studies|6.1.4.why: Trade and technology are what let civilizations grow beyond small villages — many ideas from this era, like money and writing, are still with us today.

Social Studies|6.1.5.title: Art, Writing, and Belief in Ancient Cultures
Social Studies|6.1.5.goal: You're comparing how different ancient civilizations expressed themselves through architecture, writing, and art.
Social Studies|6.1.5.why: The way people write, build, and create tells us what they valued — it's like reading a civilization's personality.

Social Studies|6.1.6.title: Early Forms of Government
Social Studies|6.1.6.goal: You'll compare different types of early government — monarchy, democracy, oligarchy, theocracy — and see how they compare to governments today.
Social Studies|6.1.6.why: Almost every government today borrows ideas from these ancient systems, including the one you live under.

Social Studies|6.2.1.title: What Do the World's Religions Believe?
Social Studies|6.2.1.goal: You're getting a closer look at the core beliefs of the major world religions.
Social Studies|6.2.1.why: These belief systems shaped laws, art, and conflicts for centuries — and still guide billions of people's lives today.

Social Studies|6.2.2.title: Religion Spreads and Connects the World
Social Studies|6.2.2.goal: You'll see how the spread of religious ideas — through trade, conquest, and events like the Crusades — connected distant parts of the world.
Social Studies|6.2.2.why: This is one of the first times in history the world starts feeling “globalized” — ideas moving across huge distances.

Social Studies|6.2.3.title: Big Inventions of the Middle Ages
Social Studies|6.2.3.goal: You're learning about major inventions from 500–1500 CE, like the printing press and new medical and astronomical tools.
Social Studies|6.2.3.why: Some of these inventions changed how fast information could travel — a big deal before the internet existed.

Social Studies|6.2.4.title: Geography and Global Connection
Social Studies|6.2.4.goal: You'll trace how geography allowed trade routes, ideas, and even diseases to spread between distant regions.
Social Studies|6.2.4.why: The same routes that carried silk and spices also carried the Black Death — geography connects both good and bad.

Social Studies|6.2.5.title: Government Moves Toward Self-Rule
Social Studies|6.2.5.goal: You're seeing how power slowly shifted away from single all-powerful rulers, through things like the Magna Carta and feudalism.
Social Studies|6.2.5.why: This is an early step toward the idea that ordinary people should have rights and a say in government.

Social Studies|6.2.6.title: Trade Connects the World's Cultures
Social Studies|6.2.6.goal: You'll see how the exchange of goods and ideas gave China, India, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia huge influence on the wider world.
Social Studies|6.2.6.why: Global trade networks from this era are the ancestors of the interconnected world you live in today.

Social Studies|6.3.1.title: Exploration and Colonization Begin
Social Studies|6.3.1.goal: You're looking at why European powers began exploring and colonizing other parts of the world.
Social Studies|6.3.1.why: These choices reshaped the map of the world and set up conflicts that are still relevant today.

Social Studies|6.3.2.title: The Lasting Impact of Colonization
Social Studies|6.3.2.goal: You'll examine some of the long-term effects that exploration and colonization had on the world.
Social Studies|6.3.2.why: Understanding these impacts helps explain many of today's global inequalities and conflicts.

Social Studies|6.3.3.title: Winners, Losers, and the Industrial Revolution
Social Studies|6.3.3.goal: You're weighing the positive and negative economic effects of global expansion and the Industrial Revolution — including the Columbian Exchange and the slave trade.
Social Studies|6.3.3.why: Big economic shifts always create winners and losers — this standard asks you to think critically about both sides.

Social Studies|6.3.4.title: Revolutions Change the World
Social Studies|6.3.4.goal: You'll study the causes and effects of major revolutions from the 1700s–1900s, from France to Latin America to India.
Social Studies|6.3.4.why: These revolutions introduced ideas about freedom and self-government that still shape politics today.

Social Studies|6.3.5.title: World War I, the Depression, and World War II
Social Studies|6.3.5.goal: You're covering the causes and effects of two world wars and the Great Depression in between them.
Social Studies|6.3.5.why: This is one of the most consequential 30-year stretches in modern history — it reshaped the entire globe.

Social Studies|6.4.1.title: Major Events of the Modern World
Social Studies|6.4.1.goal: You'll look at significant 20th and 21st century events — from the Cold War to genocides to terrorism — that shaped the world we live in now.
Social Studies|6.4.1.why: These events explain a lot about international relationships and conflicts happening in the news today.

Social Studies|6.4.2.title: Comparing Economic Systems
Social Studies|6.4.2.goal: You're comparing communism, capitalism, and socialism, and thinking about how each relates to freedom and fairness.
Social Studies|6.4.2.why: These systems are still argued about today — understanding the basics helps you follow real-world debates.

Social Studies|6.4.3.title: Human Rights Over Time
Social Studies|6.4.3.goal: You'll trace how ideas about human rights have developed and look at efforts to protect them.
Social Studies|6.4.3.why: Many rights people take for granted today were fought for fairly recently — it's worth knowing that history.

Social Studies|6.4.4.title: The World Today, Connected
Social Studies|6.4.4.goal: You're finding a current news story that shows how connected the modern world really is.
Social Studies|6.4.4.why: This closes out the year by connecting everything you've learned to what's actually happening right now.

Science|6.1.1.title: The Sun-Earth-Moon System
Science|6.1.1.goal: You're modeling how the Sun, Earth, and Moon interact to create moon phases, eclipses, and the seasons.
Science|6.1.1.why: These patterns explain everyday things you can actually go outside and observe.

Science|6.1.2.title: Gravity and Orbits
Science|6.1.2.goal: You'll explore how gravity and inertia work together to keep planets and moons in orbit.
Science|6.1.2.why: The same forces that keep satellites and the Moon in orbit are at work everywhere in the universe.

Science|6.1.3.title: Just How Big Is the Solar System?
Science|6.1.3.goal: You're using real data to compare the sizes, distances, and temperatures of solar system objects.
Science|6.1.3.why: The scale of space is almost impossible to imagine without comparing real numbers side by side.

Science|6.2.1.title: Atoms and Molecules
Science|6.2.1.goal: You'll model how atoms combine in different ways to form molecules like water and carbon dioxide.
Science|6.2.1.why: Everything physical around you — including you — is built from combinations like these.

Science|6.2.2.title: Heat and the States of Matter
Science|6.2.2.goal: You're looking at how heat energy changes matter between solid, liquid, and gas, and how that affects density.
Science|6.2.2.why: This explains everyday stuff, like why ice floats and why steam rises.

Science|6.2.3.title: Heat, Temperature, and Particle Motion
Science|6.2.3.goal: You'll investigate how temperature and heat transfer relate to how fast particles are moving.
Science|6.2.3.why: This is the science behind why some things feel hot or cold, and how heat actually moves.

Science|6.2.4.title: Conductors and Insulators
Science|6.2.4.goal: You're designing something that either speeds up or slows down heat transfer, using conductors and insulators.
Science|6.2.4.why: This is the same science behind winter coats, oven mitts, and computer cooling systems.

Science|6.3.1.title: The Water Cycle
Science|6.3.1.goal: You'll model how solar energy, gravity, and density drive the water cycle.
Science|6.3.1.why: Every drop of rain that's ever fallen has been through this same cycle, over and over, for billions of years.

Science|6.3.2.title: Air Pressure and Weather
Science|6.3.2.goal: You're investigating how high and low pressure air masses interact to cause weather changes.
Science|6.3.2.why: This is literally what's happening every time the weather forecast changes.

Science|6.3.3.title: Wind, Circulation, and Regional Climate
Science|6.3.3.goal: You'll model how uneven heating of the Earth drives wind patterns and creates regional climate effects, including Utah's own lake-effect snow and inversions.
Science|6.3.3.why: This explains why the weather where you live behaves the way it does.

Science|6.3.4.title: The Greenhouse Effect
Science|6.3.4.goal: You're exploring how the greenhouse effect keeps Earth's temperature balanced, and comparing it to Venus and Mars.
Science|6.3.4.why: This is the core science behind one of the most talked-about topics today: climate change.

Science|6.4.1.title: Populations and Resources
Science|6.4.1.goal: You'll analyze how the availability of resources affects the size of populations in an ecosystem.
Science|6.4.1.why: This explains why animal populations rise and fall, and it's central to understanding conservation.

Science|6.4.2.title: How Species Interact
Science|6.4.2.goal: You're learning about competition, predation, and mutualism — the different ways species interact with each other.
Science|6.4.2.why: Every ecosystem is really just a giant, ongoing web of relationships like these.

Science|6.4.3.title: Food Webs and Energy Flow
Science|6.4.3.goal: You'll model how matter and energy move through an ecosystem via food webs — producers, consumers, and decomposers.
Science|6.4.3.why: This is the foundation for understanding how ecosystems stay balanced, or don't.

Science|6.4.4.title: When Ecosystems Change
Science|6.4.4.goal: You're arguing how changes to an ecosystem affect the stability of its populations.
Science|6.4.4.why: This connects directly to real-world issues like invasive species and habitat loss.

Science|6.4.5.title: Protecting Biodiversity
Science|6.4.5.goal: You'll evaluate real design solutions — like wildlife corridors — for protecting ecosystems and biodiversity.
Science|6.4.5.why: This is where all your ecosystem knowledge turns into thinking about real conservation solutions.

An owl can rotate its head up to 270 degrees without hurting itself.
A butterfly tastes with its feet.
Honeybees tell each other where to find food by doing a special "waggle dance."
An ant can lift objects up to 50 times its own body weight.
Some spiders can "fly" by releasing silk threads and floating on the wind — it's called ballooning.

Snakes smell with their tongues, not their noses.

Sea otters hold hands while sleeping so they don't drift apart from each other.
A seal can slow its heartbeat down to just a few beats per minute while diving.

A ladybug can eat over 5,000 insects in its lifetime.

Koalas sleep up to 20 hours a day.

A polar bear's skin is actually black underneath all that white fur.

A wild boar's tusks never stop growing throughout its life.
Pigs are considered one of the smartest animals, smarter than most dogs.

Baby goats, called kids, can develop regional "accents" based on the other goats around them.

No two zebras have the exact same stripe pattern — like fingerprints.

Rats are ticklish and even laugh, though at a pitch too high for humans to hear.

Swans can bend their necks into an S-shape because they have more neck bones than a giraffe.
Wild turkeys can run up to 25 mph and fly in short, powerful bursts.
A rooster doesn't actually need sunlight to know when to crow.
Some parrots can live over 80 years, easily outliving their owners.
Hummingbirds are the only birds that can fly backwards.
A woodpecker's tongue wraps almost all the way around the inside of its skull to cushion its brain.

A peacock's iconic "eye" feathers are used to attract mates during a dance-like display.
A pufferfish inflates by gulping huge amounts of water, swelling to several times its normal size.

A mantis shrimp can punch so fast it briefly creates a flash of light and heat.

A quokka is famous for looking like it's always smiling, earning it the nickname "world's happiest animal."

A tarantula can survive over two years without eating.
A banana slug can grow up to 10 inches long, making it one of the largest slugs in the world.
An alligator's bite force is one of the strongest of any animal, but the muscles that open its jaw are surprisingly weak.
A walrus can use its tusks to haul its huge body out of icy water, kind of like ice picks.

funfact.text: There are more possible ways to play a game of chess than atoms in the observable universe.

A day on Venus is longer than a year on Venus.
Your brain uses about 20% of your body's total energy, even though it's only about 2% of your body weight.
White chocolate isn't technically chocolate — it contains no cocoa solids.
More people have traveled to space than have visited the deepest part of the ocean.
Your teeth start forming before you're even born.
A bolt of lightning is roughly five times hotter than the surface of the sun.
Mount Everest grows about 4 millimeters taller every year.
Bananas are naturally a tiny bit radioactive because of their potassium — completely harmless to eat.
The Library of Congress adds around 12,000 new items to its collection every single day.
The Moon is slowly drifting away from Earth, about 1.5 inches every year.
Hot water can sometimes freeze faster than cold water — a puzzle scientists still study.

Scotland's official national animal is the unicorn.

A single teaspoon of a neutron star would weigh about as much as a mountain.
The color orange was named after the fruit, not the other way around.
Some spider silk is stronger, ounce for ounce, than steel.
The dot over a lowercase "i" or "j" has its own name: a tittle.

Apples float in water because they're made up of about 25% air.

Carrots were originally purple before farmers bred the familiar orange variety.
